associated_with.note: The camp ground of the 1812 camp records; which lodge each family had is not recorded.

not_in_this_household.note: Everyone the T-3463..T-3467 day readings put in this household is on the card (liberty L-1812-town-days-3463).

persons.name: A man of the camp by the creek mouth, a canoe man (name not recorded)

age_band.note: Chosen to give the drawn camp a believable spread of ages; not recorded.

present_on_scene_date.note: Helm counts 500 warriors and 179 women and children at the gathering; this card stands for some of them. No source takes a roll call on the afternoon of 14 August 1812; this is read from the evidence below.

persons.note: A representative figure, not a recorded individual. No Potawatomi name is given because none is recorded; inventing one would present fiction as evidence. In the town from 1803-07-01 to 1812-08-16: Two roles. (1) At the gathering, 12-16 August 1812, as every camp card (the camp records). (2) Before it, the ordinary visitors who came and went by habit (Currey), by day only and in the trading seasons, away in winter. From the fort's first summer (1803).

evidence.locator: App. VI, Helm's narrative (1814), Gutenberg #69274 lines 16635-16636
evidence.quote: the tribes there assembled to amount of 500 warriors 179 women & children
evidence.claim: Helm's count of the gathering at Wells's council.

evidence.quote: while in this vicinity they lived in their wigwams near the river, their favorite camping place being at a point on the south bank
evidence.claim: Their usual camping place was the State Street creek on the south bank.

evidence.quote: beyond which were the groups of Indian wigwams clustered along the creek
evidence.claim: The wigwams along the creek, seen from the fort on the last day.

evidence.quote: The Indians continued to come and go on their nomadic excursions according to their habit
evidence.claim: Before 1812 the Potawatomi came and went at Chicago as a habit.

evidence.quote: the Indians also brought in quantities of maple sugar put up in birch-bark packages
evidence.claim: Furs and maple sugar brought in for trade.

evidence.quote: carried with them to their wintering-grounds, to be brought back in the spring, when they returned to make their corn-fields
evidence.claim: Families left their summer villages for winter hunting grounds and came back in spring (Juliette Kinzie's own observation, on the road to Chicago, March 1831).

persons.name: A man of the camp by the creek mouth (name not recorded)

age_band.note: Chosen to give the drawn camp a believable spread of ages; not recorded.

present_on_scene_date.note: Helm counts 500 warriors and 179 women and children at the gathering; this card stands for some of them. No source takes a roll call on the afternoon of 14 August 1812; this is read from the evidence below.

persons.note: A representative figure, not a recorded individual. No Potawatomi name is given because none is recorded; inventing one would present fiction as evidence. In the town from 1812-08-12 to 1812-08-16: The gathering: Heald has the neighbours come in from all quarters after the order of 9 August; the camp records stand 12 to 16 August (the council of the 12th to the burning of the fort, L-1812-potawatomi-camp-2515). Before the 12th no lodge is drawn, and after the 16th the gathering broke up (no source dates it), so the card is shown 12 to 16 August only.
